newsitem.title: UK: UK trade union bank reports sharp rise in profits.
newsitem.headline: UK trade union bank reports sharp rise in profits.

text.p: Britain's trade union owned Unity Trust Bank said on Tuesday that group pretax profit for 1996 had increased by 137 percent to 1.283 million stg from 541,000 stg in 1995.
Unity Trust Bank is 64 percent owned by trades unions with 35.9 percent owned by Britian's Co-operative Bank, itself a subsidiary of the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS).
Pre-tax profit at the bank itself rose by 10 percent to 729,000 stg. It said interest income had risen by nearly 10 percent "thanks to a steady increase in current account balances".
It said it had continued to develop its customer base in the so-called "social economy" -- including charities, co-operatives and other similar organisations.
Unity said retail deposits from this market now accounting for 30 percent of its total, and it intended to continue this diversification.
Its board recommended a dividend 1.0 pence per ordinary share. It did not pay a dividend in 1995.
Unity's share of losses from financial services company Unity Financial Holdings, which it owns jointly with Colonial Group, fell to 106,000 stg in 1996 from 549,000 stg a year before.
Jacques Martin Unity, which is developing industry-wide pension schemes and providing independent pensions consultancy for trades unions, reduced its losses to 216,000 stg from 248,000 stg.
Unity Investment Management increased its fee income by 13 percent to 516,000 stg and funds under management rose to 159.6 million stg by the end of 1996 from 136.2 million stg at the start.

Sir Dennis Landau, Unity's chairman, said that while Britain's Conservative and Labour parties' proposals to reform the state pensions were a step in the right direction but did not go far enough in addressing the problems of an ageing population and an out-of-date pensions system.

He said retiring workers could only be confident of secure and adequate pensions if a new government introduced compulsory contributions to a second-tier pesnion at a level well above that of the current SERPS (state earnings related pension scheme) rebate.
